kettlebell.title: First time with a kettlebell
kettlebell.intro: A kettlebell puts the weight below your hand, which makes it uniquely good at teaching your hips to produce power and your core to resist being pulled around. Learn how it behaves first, and everything after it goes faster.

points.heading: The parts of the bell
points.body: The handle is the metal loop on top. Its two curved sides are the horns. The round mass underneath is the bell or ball. Weights are in kilograms.

points.heading: It is not a dumbbell
points.body: The mass hangs below your hand, not around it. That offset makes the bell pull, tip and keep travelling — so it must stay close to your body.

points.heading: Pick it up by hinging
points.body: Push your hips back, keep your back flat, and reach down. Never stoop with a rounded back. Set it down the same way, every single time.

points.heading: Bailing out of a rep
points.body: Never fight a bell that has gone wrong. Let go and step back — floors survive dropped bells, backs and wrists do not. Clear your space first.

points.heading: Picking a starting weight
points.body: Start lighter than feels impressive: 12-16 kg for hinges and rows, 6-8 kg for halos. If your form changes on rep five, the bell is too heavy.

points.heading: Wrist and grip
points.body: In racked positions the bell should rest gently on the back of your forearm, not bang the wrist bone. Keep knuckles stacked over the forearm.

kettlebell.ladderNote: The swing is a fast hinge. Each rung teaches the hinge at a higher speed, so by the time you swing, the pattern is already automatic under load.

power.title: Starting power work
power.intro: Power is force produced quickly, and it's the physical quality that fades fastest with age — roughly twice as fast as raw strength. It's also what you actually use to catch yourself when you stumble. Ten to fifteen minutes a week is enough.

points.heading: Finish sharp, not tired
points.body: The whole prescription in four words. Power work should leave you feeling quick, never wrung out. Breathless means it turned into conditioning.

points.heading: The set ends when speed drops
points.body: In strength work, slowing down is the point. Here it means the stimulus already stopped and only the risk is left. Any rep slower than the first, any landing louder than the last — set over.

points.heading: Rest longer than feels necessary
points.body: Two to three minutes between sets. If you aren't slightly bored waiting, you haven't rested enough and the next set won't be fast.

points.heading: It goes first
points.body: Straight after the warm-up, before anything else. Power is the first quality to collapse under fatigue, so a power set done at the end of a session is just a slow set.

points.heading: One new thing, then wait 48 hours
points.body: Irritation from impact usually shows up 12–24 hours later, not during. That delay is the single biggest difference from strength work, where feedback is immediate.

points.heading: Direction matters more than load
points.body: Pushing, throwing and jumping upward are gentle on your spine. Landing is what isn't — a ballistic landing runs well over ten times bodyweight through the low back. That's why this ladder looks the way it does.

power.ladderNote: Each rung earns the next. A rung isn't passed by doing it once — it's passed by doing it for a few weeks with nothing showing up the next morning.

criteria: You can produce a genuinely fast rep on command without holding your breath or jerking the start.
Every rep in a set of five looks the same speed.
Landings are silent — if you can hear it, the step is too high.
You can hold the landing position for two seconds without wobbling.
Sixty contacts in a session with nothing in your back or legs the next morning.
Landings still quiet at rep ten, not just rep one.
Your torso stays braced through the whole bout — no low-back fatigue at the end.
Take-off is symmetric and you land on the box softly, with no hesitation.
You never jump down. Step down, every single rep.
The kettlebell ladder first: deadlift, good morning, hike pass.
You feel swings in your glutes and hamstrings — not your low back. Low-back fatigue from swings is the signal to drop back a rung.

caveats: There is no controlled research on power training in people who have had a discectomy. Every ranking here is worked out from how each movement loads the spine, plus general return-to-sport guidance — it's reasoning, not evidence.

Power fades about twice as fast as strength, not the three-to-five times you'll read online. And no trial has shown power training prevents falls better than strength training does. It's a worthwhile addition, not a replacement.

Most restrictive advice online is written for the first twelve weeks after surgery and doesn't apply to you ten years out. Most permissive fitness advice is written for people with no surgical history. Neither is aimed at you.

Three things genuinely need someone watching you move rather than a rule from an app: whether your L5-S1 tolerates the shear a kettlebell swing produces, whether ballistic twisting is safe for you, and drop landings from anything above about eight inches.
